primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Darier disease due to ATP2A2 dysfunction
mechanism: ATP2A2 encodes SERCA2, an endoplasmic-reticulum Ca2+-ATPase that pumps cytosolic calcium into the ER. Reduced SERCA2 function disrupts intracellular calcium homeostasis and calcium-dependent keratinocyte adhesion/differentiation, causing acantholytic dyskeratosis and greasy hyperkeratotic papules.
vignette: A 19-year-old woman has recurrent pruritic, greasy, crusted papules over the upper chest, back, forehead, and scalp that worsen with heat and sun exposure. Nail examination shows V-shaped distal notching. Her father has similar skin disease. Biopsy demonstrates suprabasal acantholysis with dyskeratotic keratinocytes. Genetic testing identifies a heterozygous ATP2A2 pathogenic variant.
lead: Which cellular function is most directly impaired by this mutation?
correct: ATP-dependent transport of calcium from the cytosol into the endoplasmic reticulum by SERCA2
distractors: Calcium export from the Golgi apparatus by ATP2C1
Formation of desmosomal cadherin extracellular domains by DSG1
Assembly of keratin 5 and keratin 14 intermediate filaments
Anchoring of basal keratinocytes to the basement membrane by type XVII collagen
distractor_notes: ATP2C1 dysfunction causes Hailey-Hailey disease, a distinct inherited acantholytic disorder.
DSG1 defects cause other disorders of desmosomal adhesion and are not the ATP2A2/SERCA2 mechanism.
KRT5/KRT14 defects cause epidermolysis bullosa simplex rather than Darier disease.
COL17A1 defects cause junctional epidermolysis bullosa, not suprabasal acantholytic dyskeratosis from ER calcium-pump dysfunction.
key_expl: Darier disease is caused by ATP2A2 variants that impair SERCA2-mediated sequestration of calcium into the endoplasmic reticulum. Disturbed calcium signaling weakens keratinocyte adhesion and differentiation, producing acantholysis and dyskeratosis.
objective: Connect ATP2A2/SERCA2 dysfunction in Darier disease with impaired endoplasmic-reticulum calcium sequestration and keratinocyte adhesion.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
diagnosis: Kindler epidermolysis bullosa due to FERMT1 dysfunction
mechanism: FERMT1 encodes kindlin-1, a focal-adhesion adaptor involved in integrin-associated signaling and linkage of actin to membrane adhesion complexes. Loss causes mixed-level skin fragility with acral blistering early in life, childhood photosensitivity, progressive poikiloderma and skin atrophy, plus mucosal disease.
vignette: A 13-year-old girl has had trauma-induced acral blisters since infancy. During childhood she developed marked photosensitivity that has become somewhat less severe with age. Examination shows mottled hypo- and hyperpigmentation with telangiectasias and skin atrophy on the hands and feet, as well as gingivitis. Her parents are first cousins. Genetic testing identifies biallelic FERMT1 variants.
lead: Which diagnosis best explains this presentation?
distractors: Epidermolysis bullosa simplex
Dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa
Xeroderma pigmentosum
Rothmund-Thomson syndrome
distractor_notes: EBS causes mechanically induced blistering, usually from basal keratinocyte structural defects, but the combination of early acral blistering, photosensitivity, progressive poikiloderma/atrophy and FERMT1 is characteristic of Kindler EB.
Dystrophic EB is a COL7A1 anchoring-fibril disorder with sublamina-densa cleavage and scarring; FERMT1 with photosensitivity/poikiloderma points to Kindler EB.
Xeroderma pigmentosum causes extreme UV sensitivity and early skin cancers from nucleotide-excision-repair defects but not congenital trauma-induced blistering from FERMT1 loss.
Rothmund-Thomson syndrome can cause poikiloderma but is associated with RECQL4 and additional skeletal/growth abnormalities rather than inherited epidermolysis bullosa.
key_expl: Kindler syndrome is a rare epidermolysis bullosa subtype due to biallelic FERMT1 variants. The signature combination is skin fragility/blistering from infancy, prominent childhood photosensitivity, progressive poikiloderma and cutaneous atrophy, and frequent mucosal disease.
objective: Recognize Kindler epidermolysis bullosa from the combination of early trauma-induced blistering, photosensitivity, progressive poikiloderma/atrophy, mucosal disease, and FERMT1 variants.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Generalized arterial calcification of infancy due to ENPP1 deficiency
mechanism: ENPP1 converts extracellular ATP to AMP and inorganic pyrophosphate (PPi). PPi is a potent inhibitor of hydroxyapatite deposition. ENPP1 deficiency lowers extracellular PPi, permitting pathologic mineral deposition in arterial walls and causing infantile arterial calcification and stenosis.
vignette: A 2-month-old infant has severe hypertension and heart failure. CT angiography shows diffuse calcification and narrowing of the aorta, coronary arteries, and renal arteries. Serum calcium and phosphate are not elevated enough to explain the extensive calcification. Genetic testing identifies biallelic ENPP1 loss-of-function variants.
lead: Deficiency of which extracellular metabolite most directly promotes the vascular calcification?
distractors: Cyclic AMP
Uric acid
1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D
Osteoprotegerin
distractor_notes: cAMP is a second messenger but is not the direct extracellular hydroxyapatite inhibitor generated by ENPP1.
Uric acid participates in purine metabolism and does not explain ENPP1-related arterial mineralization.
Calcitriol can influence calcium/phosphate balance, but ENPP1-GACI is driven directly by deficient extracellular PPi.
Osteoprotegerin regulates osteoclastogenesis through RANKL and is not the key extracellular inhibitor lost in ENPP1 deficiency.
key_expl: ENPP1 hydrolyzes extracellular ATP to AMP and PPi. PPi inhibits hydroxyapatite deposition. Loss of ENPP1 lowers PPi and permits widespread arterial calcification and stenosis in infancy.
objective: Link ENPP1 deficiency in generalized arterial calcification of infancy to reduced extracellular pyrophosphate and loss of hydroxyapatite inhibition.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Primary hypertrophic osteoarthropathy (pachydermoperiostosis) due to impaired prostaglandin E2 catabolism
mechanism: Biallelic HPGD or SLCO2A1 variants can cause primary hypertrophic osteoarthropathy. HPGD loss reduces enzymatic PGE2 degradation, while SLCO2A1 loss impairs cellular prostaglandin uptake needed for clearance. Both mechanisms increase PGE2 exposure and produce digital clubbing, periostosis, arthropathy, and pachydermia.
vignette: A 20-year-old man has progressive enlargement of the fingertips, aching of the knees and ankles, and thickening of the facial and scalp skin. Examination shows marked digital clubbing and pachydermia. Radiographs show symmetric periosteal new bone formation along the tibiae and radii. Chest imaging and cardiopulmonary evaluation reveal no secondary cause of clubbing. His brother is similarly affected. Urinary prostaglandin E2 metabolites are elevated.
lead: Which biochemical abnormality most likely underlies this hereditary disorder?
correct: Impaired prostaglandin E2 degradation or transport leading to increased prostaglandin E2 exposure
distractors: Excess growth hormone secretion from a pituitary somatotroph adenoma
Deficient vascular endothelial growth factor production in distal digits
Failure of collagen type I hydroxylation due to vitamin C deficiency
Excess parathyroid hormone secretion causing subperiosteal bone resorption
distractor_notes: Acromegaly can cause coarse facial features and enlarged extremities but does not explain familial clubbing plus symmetric periostosis and elevated prostaglandin metabolites.
Clubbing and PHO are associated with increased prostaglandin signaling, not deficient VEGF as the primary inherited mechanism.
Scurvy causes defective collagen, bleeding, and impaired osteoid formation rather than pachydermia with clubbing/periostosis.
Hyperparathyroidism causes subperiosteal bone resorption, not proliferative periostosis and hereditary pachydermoperiostosis.
key_expl: Primary hypertrophic osteoarthropathy/pachydermoperiostosis is genetically linked to HPGD and SLCO2A1, both involved in PGE2 clearance. Reduced degradation or transport raises PGE2 exposure and promotes clubbing, periostosis, arthropathy, and skin thickening.
objective: Connect hereditary pachydermoperiostosis with impaired HPGD/SLCO2A1-dependent prostaglandin E2 clearance rather than secondary cardiopulmonary clubbing.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Netherton syndrome due to SPINK5 dysfunction
mechanism: SPINK5 encodes LEKT1, a serine-protease inhibitor in the epidermis. Loss of LEKT1 permits excessive epidermal protease activity, disrupting stratum-corneum barrier proteins and producing ichthyosis, hair-shaft defects such as trichorrhexis invaginata, and marked atopy.
vignette: A 4-year-old girl has chronic erythematous scaly skin, severe atopic disease, elevated IgE, and recurrent allergic symptoms. Hair microscopy shows trichorrhexis invaginata ('bamboo hair'). Genetic testing identifies biallelic SPINK5 pathogenic variants.
lead: Loss of which normal protein function most directly causes the skin-barrier defect?
correct: Inhibition of epidermal serine proteases by LEKT1
distractors: Transport of zinc into enterocytes by ZIP4
Formation of keratin 1 and keratin 10 intermediate filaments
Nucleotide-excision repair of ultraviolet-induced DNA damage
Attachment of basal keratinocytes to laminin through alpha-6-beta-4 integrin
distractor_notes: ZIP4/SLC39A4 defects cause acrodermatitis enteropathica rather than bamboo hair with the SPINK5/atopy phenotype.
KRT1/KRT10 defects cause epidermolytic ichthyosis, not Netherton syndrome.
Nucleotide-excision-repair defects cause xeroderma pigmentosum and UV-induced malignancy risk.
Integrin attachment defects cause junctional epidermolysis bullosa rather than excessive protease activity and trichorrhexis invaginata.
key_expl: SPINK5 encodes LEKT1, an epidermal serine-protease inhibitor. LEKT1 deficiency causes uncontrolled protease activity, defective stratum-corneum barrier function, ichthyosis, trichorrhexis invaginata, and atopy.
objective: Link SPINK5/LEKT1 deficiency in Netherton syndrome to excessive epidermal serine-protease activity and impaired skin-barrier integrity.
